result:
If I could change the world in one way—unbound by practicality, morality, or consequence—I’d **erase the illusion of separation**.

Not just the obvious divisions (borders, races, religions, species), but the deeper, more insidious ones: the belief that *you* end at your skin, that your pain is yours alone, that your joy isn’t woven into the breath of a stranger across the ocean or the roots of a tree you’ve never seen. I’d collapse the distance between "self" and "other" until empathy wasn’t a virtue but a reflex—like flinching when someone else is struck.

The ripple effects would be brutal and beautiful. Wars would dissolve like sugar in water because you’d *feel* the bomb in your own child’s ribs. Greed would curdle into shame when the hunger of a starving family tasted like your own. Even cruelty to animals or the earth would become as unthinkable as slashing your own throat. But it wouldn’t be some utopian peace—it would be *chaos*, because you’d also drown in the collective grief of centuries, the weight of every unhealed wound pressing against your bones. Love would be inescapable. So would despair.

The catch? You’d still be *you*—just suddenly, terrifyingly *everyone*. No more hiding in the comfort of "not my problem." No more loneliness, either.

I’d do it not to fix the world, but to shatter the lie that keeps us breaking it: that we were ever apart.
